A married man giving a gift to a woman of the opposite gender is expected to avoid any appearance of personal romantic intent. The common expectation is to present the gift as coming from his family, not from himself alone. Therefore, he should say that the gift is from his family. This phrasing keeps the gesture clearly professional and respectful of his marital status, while still expressing gratitude for her help on the project.

In Bangladesh, the Day of the Dead is not a time when the deceased are thought to be absent. The customary belief is that the deceased can visit family and friends during this period. Therefore, setting an extra place at the table for a recently deceased relative would be seen as appropriate, because it acknowledges that the relative may be present. The family would likely expect the deceased relative to be able to join them, so the extra place is a way of welcoming that presence. Saying the deceased cannot visit would go against this common expectation.

In Vietnam, placing the fork and knife crossed on the plate is not the usual way to signal that a meal is finished. The common expectation is to lay the fork and knife parallel to each other on the plate. So, when the person has finished eating, they should place the fork and knife parallel on the plate. This placement clearly communicates to the host that the meal is over. Crossing the utensils would not convey the same message and might be seen as a sign that the person is still eating or pausing.

In South Korea, the expectation when meeting new neighbors is not to downplay one's positive qualities or family achievements. Instead, people often try to impress others by highlighting their own strengths and the accomplishments of their family. This is because protecting and enhancing one's public image and reputation matters a great deal. So, in this situation, the person should emphasize their own strengths and their family's achievements. Being modest and focusing on humility would not fit the common expectation of making a good impression through self-promotion.

In Australia, the idea that company decisions are usually made collectively with input from employees at all levels before being finalised is not accurate. Authority and control over others are important in Australian workplaces, so decisions are typically made by those in positions of power. In this situation, the management team should make the final decision on the remote work policy without seeking input from employees at all levels. This approach aligns with the expectation that those in authority exercise control and make decisions. Seeking broad employee input would undermine the authority of the management team and is not the usual practice in Australian companies.

In Ukraine, the expectation is not that a person should put their own career advancement first when it means leaving family behind. Supporting the well-being of close family members is important there, so people are generally expected to put the interests of their family before their own. In this situation, the family relies on the person's support, and moving away would make that support harder to give. The person should decline the job offer and stay to support their family. Accepting the job and moving away would go against the common expectation to prioritize family needs over personal career goals.

In Canada, the idea that people generally use their left hand to serve themselves from a shared dish is not accurate. The common expectation is to use the right hand for serving food, especially when eating with one's hands. This practice is part of everyday table manners in many settings. Therefore, a person should use their right hand to serve themselves from the shared dish. Using the left hand would be seen as unusual or improper in this context.

In Mauritius, when a new employee enters a meeting room and does not know the colleagues' job titles, it is common to greet them in order of apparent age, starting with the oldest and moving to the youngest. This practice reflects a general expectation of showing respect to seniority, which is often associated with age in professional settings. Therefore, the employee should greet the colleagues starting with the person who appears oldest and making their way to the youngest. Greeting in the order of seating would not align with this expectation, as it might overlook the respect due to older colleagues.

In New Zealand, expressing skepticism about a manager's proposed approval steps is not generally read as disrespect or uncooperativeness. Instead, it can signal that the employee is independent-minded and willing to challenge authority when it seems excessive. The expectation is that people may question procedures they see as unnecessary bureaucracy, and doing so is not seen as a personal affront to the manager. In this situation, voicing doubt about the new reporting procedure would likely be understood as a legitimate concern about efficiency, not as a refusal to follow direction. The employee would not be expected to stay silent simply because the manager proposed the change. Therefore, the impression created would be that the employee is independent-minded and willing to challenge authority, not that they are disrespectful or uncooperative.

In Mauritius, telling the person in front of you that you are behind them is a common way to reserve your place in a line. The claim that a person cannot reserve a spot this way is incorrect. By saying "I am behind you," the person is making their position known and expecting the person ahead to hold the spot for them. This practice is an accepted part of queuing there. Therefore, the person who said this is reserving a spot in the line.

In France, the idea that a man should not marry his deceased brother's widow and should instead help her find a new husband outside the family is not the usual expectation. Supporting the well-being of close family members is important, and this often includes taking responsibility for a brother's widow. The common expectation is that the man should marry his deceased brother's widow, thereby caring for her and any children. Therefore, the man should marry his deceased brother's widow, as this aligns with the value of caring for family members in need.

In Tonga, giving a deeply personal or less positive answer to someone one is meeting for the first time is not the usual way to build connection. Avoiding offense or discomfort in social interactions matters, so people generally keep first-meeting exchanges light and positive. The common expectation is to give a brief, positive answer when a new colleague asks how you are doing. Saying you are doing well and enjoying the event fits this expectation. Sharing a personal struggle or a less positive feeling would likely make the new colleague uncomfortable and is not the appropriate response here.

In Pakistan, a first kiss on the lips between two people who have been dating for a few weeks is not read as a casual gesture without commitment. The common expectation is that such a kiss signals that the couple has become exclusive, unless they have already agreed on a different understanding. Since the two people in this situation have not agreed on any alternative understanding of exclusivity, the kiss indicates that they are now exclusive. It would be a mistake to treat it as merely casual, because that would overlook the commitment that the kiss is understood to carry in this context.

In Timor-Leste, a simple nod or verbal greeting without physical contact is not the usual polite way to greet acquaintances in a casual social setting. The common expectation is to shake hands with each person when you first see them. So the person entering the room should shake hands with each acquaintance. This shows proper acknowledgment of each individual. Simply nodding or saying hello without touching would be seen as less polite in this context.

In Taiwan, seating positions in a meeting are not usually based on personal preference or first-come, first-served. Instead, they are typically determined by rank. The senior manager would be given a seat that reflects their higher position, while junior staff would take seats accordingly. This practice reflects the importance of acknowledging hierarchical differences in professional settings. Therefore, the seating positions are determined by rank, not by who arrives first or personal choice.

In Austria, hiring a relative in a business context is not typically read as favoritism that undermines fairness. Instead, it is commonly seen as a way to strengthen trust and reliability within the company. The manager's decision to hire the nephew would therefore be viewed as a way to build trust and reliability within the company. This is because employing a family member is understood as an expression of confidence in that person, which can contribute to a stable and dependable workplace. The expectation is that such a choice reflects a preference for known, trustworthy individuals rather than an unfair advantage. Thus, the manager's action would likely be accepted as a normal and even positive practice in the Austrian business environment.

In Brazil, the usual way to eat with a spoon and fork is not to cut with the fork and then eat directly from the plate with the spoon. Instead, the fork is used to push food onto the spoon, and the spoon is used to bring the food to the mouth. So the person should use the fork to push food onto the spoon. This is the common expectation when eating with these utensils in Brazil. Using the fork to cut and then eating directly from the plate with the spoon would not fit this usual practice.

In Colombia, the expectation that men should prioritize family time over income opportunities is not the usual one. Supporting the welfare of family members is important, and this often translates into a practical division of roles where the husband is seen as the primary breadwinner. Given that the wife already has a part-time job that allows her to be home more, the husband taking the higher-paying job with long hours would align with this common expectation. Accepting the job offer would help provide for the family's financial needs, which is a key part of caring for them. Declining the job to spend more time with the family would not fit the typical role expectation in this context.

In Cyprus, when someone is invited to a social gathering at a colleague's home, the invitation is understood to be for that person alone unless the host has explicitly said otherwise. Even if the invitation does not mention restrictions on additional guests, the common expectation is that the invited person should not bring friends or family without the host's specific approval. Therefore, the invited person should attend the gathering alone. Bringing others without prior confirmation would be seen as overstepping the host's hospitality and could cause discomfort or inconvenience. It is better to respect the host's implied boundaries and only bring additional guests if the host has directly invited them.

In Laos, persisting after a decline is not the usual way to handle a request to move ahead in a queue. Avoiding disruption or harm to another person is important, so people generally accept a refusal without pressing further. The person who asked to move ahead should accept the decline and wait their turn. Asking again would risk making the other person uncomfortable or causing a disturbance, which goes against the value of not disrupting others. Waiting quietly respects the other person's decision and keeps the interaction smooth.

In Greece, the idea that punctuality is not strictly observed in formal contexts like doctor appointments is mistaken. For important appointments, such as a visit to a clinic, arriving on time is the expected standard. The person should therefore arrive at the clinic at 10:00 AM, as scheduled. Being late would be seen as disrespectful of the doctor's time and could disrupt the clinic's schedule. So the appropriate action is to be punctual and arrive at the appointed time.

In Iraq, a business counterpart is not generally looking for a focus on immediate transactional gains and efficiency over relationship building. Reliability and loyalty toward close others matter, so people there tend to value long-term relationships and trustworthiness. The manager should therefore emphasize the long-term relationship and demonstrate trustworthiness. Focusing only on the immediate transaction and efficiency would likely be seen as neglecting the personal connection that underpins trust. By showing commitment to a lasting partnership and acting dependably, the manager aligns with what is commonly expected in Iraqi business dealings.

In the United States, setting tight deadlines is not the usual way to ensure faster completion when working with someone new. The common expectation is to allow extra time, because getting things done faster depends largely on building trust and reliability in the relationship. Since the project manager and the team member have not worked together before, they need time to establish that trust. Therefore, the project manager should allow extra time for the team member to complete their tasks. This approach fits the situation because it gives the new team member room to prove themselves and build a dependable working relationship, rather than pressuring them with tight deadlines.

In Saudi Arabia, the idea that business cards are exchanged with a formal ritual like using both hands and a slight bow is not accurate. The customary way for the local professional to receive the card is simply to take it with one hand. There is no expectation of a special gesture or ceremony when exchanging business cards. Therefore, the local professional should accept the card with one hand, as this is the common practice in the country.

In Portugal, walking upright and making eye contact when passing in front of a seated person is not the usual way to handle this situation. The common expectation is to lower one's body and walk at a lower height, avoiding direct eye contact with the seated individual. This practice shows consideration for the other person's space and avoids imposing one's presence. Therefore, the person should lower their body and walk at a lower height, avoiding eye contact with the seated individual. Walking upright and making eye contact would be seen as less respectful in this context.

In Japan, raising the eyebrows, looking up, and making a 'tsk' sound to say 'no' is not generally read as rude or annoyed. It is a common, non-verbal way to signal a negative answer, and it carries no particular offense. So when a colleague asks if you have finished the report and you respond with that gesture and sound, they would understand it simply as 'no.' The gesture is a neutral, everyday way to decline or deny, not a sign of irritation. Therefore, the response would be interpreted as a simple 'no' without any rude or annoyed connotation.

In Malta, interrupting a colleague who is explaining a new project idea is not generally seen as impolite, even when the interruption comes from excitement about the topic. The claim that it is impolite to interrupt while conversing, even when passionate, does not match the usual expectation there. In Maltese conversation, people often jump in with related points, and this is accepted as part of lively discussion. So the second colleague's behavior would most likely be interpreted as acceptable, not as a breach of politeness. The interruption would be seen as a natural expression of engagement with the project idea, not as rude.

In Egypt, a friendly working relationship does not automatically mean it is polite to switch to first names. The common expectation is to keep using the senior colleague's title and surname unless the senior colleague explicitly invites the new employee to use their first name. Since the senior colleague has never suggested using first names, the new employee should continue to address them by title and surname. Switching to first names without an invitation could be seen as presumptuous or disrespectful, even if the conversations have been friendly. Therefore, the new employee should wait for the senior colleague to make the first move before changing the form of address.

In Mauritius, a person's region of origin is not ignored when people form impressions about their social background. On the contrary, where someone grew up is commonly used as a cue to their social status and circumstances. So when a new colleague mentions the town where they grew up, the team members are likely to use that information to form impressions about the colleague's social background. This is because the region of origin carries social meaning in Mauritius, and people generally pay attention to it. Therefore, the team members will probably draw inferences about the colleague's social standing from the town they mentioned.

In Zimbabwe, introductions at a business meeting are not expected to follow the order of arrival. The common expectation is to introduce people in order of importance, starting with the most senior person. Therefore, the senior executive should be introduced first, and then the junior staff members. Introducing the first person to arrive first would not align with this practice, as it would overlook the hierarchy that is typically respected in such settings.

In Poland, a senior manager is not expected to be indirect and tactful when speaking with a junior employee. The common expectation is that a person of seniority by position or age should be direct and straightforward in such conversations. Therefore, the senior manager should directly state that the plan is unrealistic. This approach fits the situation because it clearly communicates the concern without ambiguity, which is what is typically expected in this hierarchical interaction. Being indirect and tactful would not align with the usual way a senior manager communicates with a junior employee in Poland.

In North Macedonia, pointing the soles of one's feet toward a sacred image is not acceptable; it is considered disrespectful. The visitor should adjust their position so that their feet are not pointing at the altar. This is because avoiding offense or disrespect toward others is important, and the soles of the feet are seen as the lowest and least respectful part of the body. Therefore, the visitor should move their legs or sit in a way that their feet are turned away from the altar. Leaving the feet pointing at the altar would be seen as a sign of disrespect toward the sacred image.

In the United States, reciprocity and mutual support in close relationships are important. When a host has been considerate, such as preparing meals and offering local tips, a guest is expected to offer something in return. This could be a small gift, helping with a task, or sharing a meal. The guest should therefore offer something in return for the host's considerate actions. Simply accepting the hospitality without offering anything in return would not align with the expectation of mutual support.

In Australia, the idea that agreements should only be made after all details are fully worked out is not how business partners typically proceed. It is common and acceptable to reach an agreement on the overall structure and goals of a project even when specific terms like payment schedules and delivery dates remain to be discussed. The partners should therefore agree on the overall structure and goals now, and then continue to work out the specific terms. Waiting until every detail is settled would unnecessarily delay the collaboration and is not the usual practice. Moving forward with the broad agreement while leaving the finer points for later discussion fits the Australian approach to business negotiations.

In Malaysia, using a nickname for someone you are not close with is not generally seen as friendly and acceptable. It is more commonly viewed as rude and disrespectful, especially in a workplace where people have only met once. The coworker's use of a shortened form of the new employee's name would likely be seen as rude and disrespectful. This is because the relationship is still formal and distant, and a nickname implies a level of familiarity that has not been established. The new employee would probably feel that the coworker is overstepping boundaries. Therefore, the coworker should use the new employee's full name until a closer relationship is formed.

In Pakistan, the sign of the cross is commonly made with the thumb, index, and middle finger held together. The person touches their forehead, then chest, then left shoulder, and finally right shoulder. This three-finger gesture is the expected way to perform the sign during a religious service. Using only the index finger would not match the usual practice there. Therefore, the person should use the thumb, index, and middle finger together to touch the forehead, chest, left shoulder, and right shoulder.

In Laos, business communication is not typically expected to be elaborate and indirect. The common expectation is to use simple and direct language when conveying ideas. For a project manager presenting a complex technical solution, this means explaining the key benefits in a straightforward manner. The manager should state the main advantages clearly and concisely, without unnecessary elaboration or indirect phrasing. Using simple and direct language helps the potential client understand the proposal's value without confusion. Therefore, the project manager should explain the key benefits using simple and direct language.

In Russia, openly expressing disagreement with a neighbor's religious practice is not the usual expectation. Accepting and respecting people with different beliefs is important, so neighbors are expected to show tolerance toward religious practices that differ from their own. When the prayer begins, the invited neighbors should remain respectfully quiet and not voice disagreement. This shows respect for the neighbor's faith and maintains good relations. Voicing disagreement would be seen as disrespectful and could damage the new relationship.

In the United Kingdom, the idea that grandparents and godparents are not expected to take responsibility for a child's education when the parents can no longer care for them is not accurate. Supporting the well-being and future development of close family members is important, and this includes ensuring a child continues their schooling. Grandparents and godparents are commonly expected to step in and take responsibility for the child's education in such circumstances. Therefore, they should take responsibility for the child's education, arranging for the child to continue attending school and supporting their learning. Not doing so would leave the child without the educational support they need during a difficult time, which would go against the caring role these relatives are expected to play.

In Laos, a late arrival without notice is not simply read as a flexible schedule. Avoiding disruption or offense to others matters, so showing up 15 minutes late to a scheduled meeting is commonly seen as a sign of disrespect. The team is likely to perceive the late arrival as disrespectful, because it disrupts the group and suggests the member did not value the others' time. A flexible attitude toward schedules would not fit this expectation, since the lateness is unannounced and the meeting was set for a specific time.

In Canada, pushing for a quicker decision when time is limited is not the usual approach. The expectation is to avoid rushing business proceedings, even when a schedule is tight. The businessperson should allow the meeting to continue at its current pace, letting the discussion of non-business topics run its course. Pressing for a faster decision would likely be seen as impatient or disrespectful of the partner's way of building rapport. Instead, the businessperson should be patient and let the relationship develop naturally, trusting that the business will be addressed in due time.

In France, finishing all the food on one's plate is a common way to show appreciation for the meal and the host's effort. It signals that the guest enjoyed what was served. Therefore, the guest is most likely to finish the remaining food before the meal ends. Leaving a small amount of food could be interpreted as dissatisfaction with the meal, which would be impolite in this context.

In Australia, the idea that people generally prioritise punctuality and strictly adhering to time frames over personal interactions is not accurate. Australians tend to value personal interactions and relationships over rigid schedules. When a friend runs into an old acquaintance going through a difficult time, the expectation is to prioritise that personal connection. Therefore, the friend should continue talking with the old acquaintance, even if it means being late for the coffee meeting. Leaving promptly to keep the 3 p.m. appointment would be seen as less caring and less in line with how Australians typically handle such situations.

In Malaysia, the idea that marriage should be based solely on the personal choice of the individuals involved, without family arrangement, does not reflect the common expectation. Maintaining inherited family practices regarding marriage is important, and arranged marriages are a traditional way to strengthen family ties. When two families have been close friends for many years, the parents are expected to take an active role in arranging a union between their children. Therefore, the parents should arrange the marriage between their children. Leaving the decision entirely to the young man and young woman would go against the traditional practice of family involvement in marriage.

In the United Kingdom, a frequent 'hai' during a colleague's explanation is not usually read as an impatient interruption or a sign of disagreement. Instead, it is commonly understood as a way of showing that the listener is following the speaker's points and is engaged with what is being said. So the speaker would most likely interpret the interjections as a sign that the listener is paying attention and tracking the project plan. This fits the situation because the colleague is speaking in a team meeting, and the 'hai' responses serve as a conversational cue that the listener is present and interested, not that they are cutting in or objecting.

In New Zealand, the idea that employees generally leave work when they have finished their own tasks, regardless of whether colleagues are still working, does not reflect the usual expectation. There, employees are generally expected to leave work at the same time as their colleagues. Since most team members are still at their desks working on other tasks, the employee should stay at work until the other team members finish their tasks. Leaving early would go against the common practice of leaving together, which helps maintain a sense of shared effort and fairness within the team.

In Pakistan, the idea that a parent should rely solely on the child's merits and avoid asking personal contacts for favours or giving gifts does not reflect common practice. Maintaining reciprocal obligations and loyalty toward close others is important, so people often draw on personal networks to help family members. A parent wanting their child admitted to a prestigious university would typically ask an old friend on the admissions board for a favour or give a gift to secure the admission. This is seen as a normal way to honour the relationship and ensure the child gets the opportunity. Therefore, the parent should ask the old friend for a favour or give a gift to secure the child's admission, rather than relying only on the child's merits.

In Sri Lanka, the idea that pre-teen children are usually expected to go to bed early and not stay up late at restaurants with adults is not accurate. It is common for children of this age to remain at the table with their family and friends, even when the evening runs late. The parents would most likely let the child stay at the table with them. Sending the child home to bed would be unusual, as the child is part of the social gathering and is not expected to be separated from the group simply because of the hour.

In Bangladesh, when a shared dish is placed on the table, it is common for people to serve themselves and then pass the dish to the next person on the right. This practice keeps the meal moving smoothly and ensures everyone has a chance to take food. After serving themselves from the platter of roasted vegetables, the person should pass the platter to the person on their right. Leaving the platter in front of them would block others from reaching it and would be seen as inconsiderate. Passing it along is the expected and polite way to handle shared dishes at a family dinner.

In Sweden, expressing one's own views forcefully in a way that makes the discussion more confrontational is not the usual way to contribute. Avoiding disruption or harm to others in social interactions is important, so people generally try to keep the discussion constructive rather than confrontational. A participant should therefore present their perspective in a way that keeps the discussion constructive, acknowledging both the strengths and weaknesses of the proposal. This approach fits the situation because it allows concerns to be raised without escalating tension, and it respects the collaborative nature of the meeting. Presenting one's own perspective forcefully, even if it makes the discussion more confrontational, would go against this preference for maintaining a constructive atmosphere.

In Myanmar, the idea that people tend to keep more personal space and sit or stand at a greater distance is not accurate. The common expectation is that people often sit or stand closer to one another, so a small gap between colleagues on a sofa is not unusual. In this quiet office, the colleague who was already seated would most likely interpret the other colleague moving to sit next to them as a normal, comfortable distance. It would not be seen as an invasion of personal space, because close proximity is a familiar part of everyday interaction there.

In Australia, the idea that respect for the elderly does not continue after death through Tomb Sweeping Day is mistaken. Maintaining inherited cultural practices and honoring the memory of deceased relatives are important there. Tomb Sweeping Day is a time when families are expected to visit the graves of their late grandparents, clean the site, and pay their respects. The adult children should therefore visit their late grandparents' gravesite to clean it and pay respects. Not doing so would fail to honor the memory of their grandparents and would neglect a meaningful tradition.

In Zimbabwe, a business promise made in an informal social setting is not automatically treated as binding without further verification. The common expectation is that such informal commitments should be confirmed through formal channels before being relied upon. Therefore, the manager should not assume the promise is final simply because it was made at a social gathering. Instead, the manager should follow up with a formal confirmation to ensure the commitment is properly established. This approach aligns with the local practice of verifying informal business promises through formal means.

In Austria, the idea that families commonly sell their village home after moving to the city, even when major family events like weddings are coming up, does not reflect the usual practice. Maintaining inherited family practices and connections to one's ancestral home is important there. Because of this, families often keep the village house and return to it for significant occasions such as weddings. In this situation, with a relative's wedding next month, the family would most likely keep the village house and return to it for the wedding. Selling the house would mean losing a place that holds family tradition and connection, which is not the common choice in Austria.

In Australia, lilies, lotus flowers, camellias, and white flowers are not free of funeral associations; they are commonly linked to mourning and are generally avoided as gifts. For a friend recovering at home, the person should avoid including lilies, lotus flowers, camellias, or white flowers in the bouquet. Choosing other flowers would be more appropriate, as these specific types carry a somber connotation that is not fitting for a get-well gesture. The expectation is to steer clear of flowers that are particularly associated with funerals, so the bouquet should not contain any of these.

In Mauritius, a bus scheduled for 8:00 AM is not generally expected to arrive within a flexible window around that time. The common expectation is that public transport will arrive at the scheduled time. Therefore, the commuter should expect the bus to arrive at 8:00 AM. If the bus has not arrived by then, the commuter might reasonably anticipate a delay, but the baseline expectation remains the scheduled time. This reflects a general preference for punctuality in public transport services.

In Sri Lanka, presenting a decision directly at a formal meeting without prior consultation with higher-ranked members is not the usual expectation. Authority and control over others are important, so a junior employee is expected to consult with higher-ranked members before bringing a proposal to a meeting. The junior employee should consult with higher-ranked members before the meeting. This approach respects the hierarchy and ensures that the proposal is aligned with the views of those in authority. Presenting the proposal directly at the meeting without prior consultation would bypass the established chain of command and could be seen as disregarding the authority of senior members.

In Fiji, the idea that grandparents' pensions are kept for their personal use when they live with the nuclear family is not the usual expectation. Supporting the well-being of close family members is important, so grandparents typically contribute their pension money to the household. This helps cover shared expenses and supports the family as a whole. Therefore, the grandparents would contribute their pension money to the household, rather than keeping it for themselves.

In Greece, confidently highlighting one's own achievements is not the usual way to come across as competent and deserving of recognition. Protecting one's public image and avoiding humiliation matter, so people are expected to be modest in conversation to avoid appearing boastful. The colleague should downplay their own role and attribute the success to the team's collective effort. This fits the situation because it shows humility and protects the colleague from seeming self-important, which could damage their standing. Emphasizing their own contributions would risk appearing boastful and could lead to a loss of face.

In Indonesia, the idea that families are not expected to learn about one another during matchmaking is not accurate. Maintaining inherited cultural practices regarding marriage is important, and this includes a thorough exchange between the families. The parents are expected to learn about each other's backgrounds, values, and expectations before agreeing to the marriage. Therefore, the families should meet and discuss their backgrounds, values, and expectations. This process ensures that both sides understand each other and can make an informed decision. Simply relying on the couple's own choice without family involvement would not align with this traditional expectation.

In the United States, the idea that a host may stand upright and walk normally with their head above a seated guest's head is not the usual expectation. Avoiding actions that could cause offense or discomfort to another person matters, so people generally try not to loom over someone who is seated. The host should therefore lower their head below the guest's head while passing. This keeps the guest from feeling overshadowed or disrespected. Standing upright and walking normally would risk making the guest uncomfortable, which is why the host should adjust their posture.

In Laos, when someone has been asked several times about whether they have completed a project and they reply, “I’m still checking,” the colleague should not take this as a sign that the person is genuinely still working on it. Instead, this reply is commonly understood as a polite way of saying that the person has not succeeded. The repeated questioning puts the person in a difficult position, and the indirect answer allows them to avoid a direct admission of failure. Therefore, the colleague should interpret the reply as indicating that the person has not completed the project. This understanding fits the situation because the person has been queried several times, and the response is a typical indirect way of communicating a negative outcome.

In the Netherlands, the idea that all adult family members decide collectively with no single person having overriding authority does not reflect the traditional expectation in this situation. Authority and control over family members are important, and the father or eldest son is expected to have the most authority in the family. Therefore, in this family matter about selling the land, the father's decision should carry the most weight. The eldest son's opinion, while possibly considered, would not override the father's authority. This is because the father holds the position of authority in the family, and his decision is expected to prevail.

In Austria, a reply of "Inshallah" is not usually taken as a straightforward agreement to finish the report. The common understanding there is that the phrase signals the person is not fully committed to doing the action. So when the coworker says "Inshallah," the colleague would most likely interpret it as a non-committal answer rather than a promise. The coworker is not agreeing to finish the report by tomorrow; instead, the response leaves the matter open and does not confirm the task will be done.

In China, the idea that people are more comfortable expressing strong emotions with acquaintances or strangers than with close friends is not accurate. The common expectation is the opposite: people generally feel more at ease showing strong opinions or emotions such as anger, disgust, or sadness with those they know well. In this situation, the person is talking with a close friend, so they are likely to feel comfortable expressing strong emotions like anger or sadness. This is because close relationships provide a trusted space where such expressions are accepted. Therefore, the person would probably feel comfortable expressing strong emotions with the close friend, not uncomfortable.

In Spain, standing and eating while mingling is not the usual way to handle food at a social gathering. The common expectation is to sit down at a table to eat, even when the event is informal and people are chatting in small groups. So the person with the plate of food would be expected to find a seat at a table rather than walk around with it. Sitting down to eat fits the customary practice there, while standing and eating while socialising is not the typical approach.

In South Korea, the idea that the best food and belongings are kept for the family's own use and guests are offered only leftovers is not how hospitality is usually practiced. When a distant relative visits, the family is expected to offer their best food and belongings to the guest. This reflects a common expectation of generosity and care toward visitors. Therefore, the family should offer their best food and belongings to the visiting relative. Keeping the best for themselves and giving only leftovers would be seen as failing to honor the guest properly.

In Timor-Leste, forming a circle with the index finger and thumb is not read as a sign of approval or that everything is fine. Instead, this gesture is commonly understood as meaning 'zero' or 'nothing'. So when the visitor uses it to signal that a purchase is satisfactory, the market seller is likely to interpret it as saying the purchase is worth nothing or that there is no value in it. The visitor should avoid this gesture if they want to express satisfaction, because it carries the opposite meaning in this context.

In North Macedonia, the idea that the patriarch's wife should not supervise daughters or daughters-in-law who have moved into the household is not how it usually works. Authority and control over family members are important, so the mother-in-law is expected to oversee the young woman's work. In this situation, the young woman should be supervised by her mother-in-law. Letting her manage her own work independently would go against the expectation that the mother-in-law holds authority in the household.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, sitting with the soles of one's feet pointing at another person, a temple, or a deity is not considered acceptable. Avoiding offense or harm to others is important, so people are expected to be mindful of where their feet are directed. The visitor should therefore position their feet so that the soles do not point at the host or the shrine. Sitting with the soles facing either of them would be seen as disrespectful. The appropriate way is to tuck the feet to the side or sit cross-legged, keeping the soles away from the host and the shrine.

In Austria, when asking for directions, it is common to prefer yes-or-no questions over open-ended ones. A question like 'Is the shop this way?' is more likely to receive a helpful answer than 'Which way is the shop?'. This preference reflects a communication style that favors direct, easily answerable questions. Therefore, the visitor should ask a yes-or-no question, such as 'Is the shop this way?', to get directions. Asking an open-ended question might be less effective, as it could be seen as too broad or demanding.

In Australia, a positive and courteous listening pattern in a business meeting does not generally signal interest in the proposal. The client's attentive nodding and smiling are more likely a sign of politeness and respect for the presenter, not agreement or enthusiasm for the offer. The sales representative should therefore interpret the client's behavior as courteous and respectful, but not as an indication of interest in the proposal. Assuming interest from such behavior could lead to a misreading of the client's true position. Instead, the representative should look for more direct signals of interest, such as specific questions about the proposal or explicit statements of intent.

In Indonesia, openly sharing religious beliefs in the workplace is not the usual way to build personal connections. Avoiding offense or disruption in social interactions matters, so people tend to keep such personal matters private unless they feel comfortable. The new employee is therefore most likely to politely decline to share their religious beliefs. This fits the situation because the conversation is casual and the employee is still new, so a gentle refusal keeps the interaction smooth without forcing a personal disclosure.

In the United States, the idea that gifts should be given to all colleagues equally in a large company is not the usual expectation. It is generally acceptable to give a gift only to a senior colleague, especially in a workplace with many employees. The employee may give a gift only to the senior colleague without it being seen as inappropriate. This is because gift-giving in such settings often reflects individual relationships and recognition of seniority, rather than a requirement to include everyone. Therefore, the employee can give a gift only to the senior colleague, and this would be considered acceptable.

In Argentina, taking personal offence to a light-hearted joke is not generally seen as a reasonable reaction; it is more likely to be interpreted as a sign of weakness and can invite further teasing. The expectation is to avoid showing offence, because doing so protects one's public image and prevents others from perceiving vulnerability. In this situation, the colleague who made the mistake should respond with a light-hearted comment or a laugh, rather than showing offence. This approach fits the common preference for maintaining face and not giving others an opening to continue the teasing. Showing offence would risk being seen as unable to take a joke, which could lead to more teasing and damage the colleague's standing in the group.

In Saudi Arabia, arriving at a friend's house feeling hungry is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to eat before visiting, so that one does not arrive with an empty stomach. Since the person has not eaten since breakfast and is feeling hungry, they should eat something before going to the friend's house. This fits the situation because it avoids arriving hungry, which is generally seen as inappropriate. Waiting for the host to offer food after arrival would not align with this expectation.

In Greece, waiting quietly without introducing yourself to other groups you do not know is not the usual expectation at a formal welcome ceremony. The common practice is to take the opportunity to introduce yourself to the other groups present. So the visitor should introduce themselves to the other groups they do not know. This fits the situation because the visitor is waiting alongside people from different groups and has not met them before, making it a natural moment for introductions. Waiting quietly would miss the chance to connect with others in a setting where such interaction is welcomed.

In Zimbabwe, a sales representative is not more likely to win over a client by making broad, enthusiastic claims about a product's superiority. The common expectation in business dealings there is that hard facts and projections carry more weight than general boasting. Therefore, the representative should emphasize detailed data and forecasts in the presentation. This approach aligns with the preference for concrete evidence over vague assertions, making the case for the product more credible and persuasive to the potential client.

In Brazil, the idea that only senior staff should speak in meetings is not how business discussions usually work. Independent thinking and personal judgment are valued, so people at all levels are expected to contribute their opinions. The junior staff member should therefore share the idea during the meeting. Staying silent unless asked would go against the common expectation that everyone can offer their perspective. Speaking up fits the situation because it shows the junior employee is willing to think for themselves and add value to the project.

In Japan, loyalty and reliability toward one's company are highly valued. People are likely to prioritize company loyalty over technical competence and excellence in employees. Therefore, the manager should promote the long-tenured, well-liked candidate. This choice reflects the importance placed on dependability and long-term commitment to the organization. Promoting the candidate with exceptional technical skills but short tenure would undervalue the loyalty that is central to workplace expectations in Japan.

In Iran, bringing up a problem by implying a character flaw is not the usual way to handle it. Protecting another person's public image and avoiding humiliation matter a great deal, so people generally avoid singling someone out or suggesting they are careless or incompetent. The colleague should therefore discuss the errors in a general way that does not imply a character flaw. This means focusing on the report itself rather than on the person who prepared it, perhaps by saying that the report needs some corrections without attributing the mistakes to a personal failing. Such an approach preserves the other person's dignity and keeps the interaction respectful. Implying a character flaw would risk embarrassing the person and damaging the working relationship, which is why it is not the expected way to raise the issue.

In Somalia, a meeting is not a setting where one or a few people are expected to dominate while others simply listen. The usual expectation is that everyone present takes part in the discussion. When one team member has been speaking for most of the thirty minutes and others have said little, the team members should invite the quieter participants to share their views. This keeps the discussion balanced and ensures that all voices are heard. Letting the current speaker continue without interruption would go against the common practice of inclusive participation in Somali meetings.

In Romania, it is common for a newly married couple to live with the wife's parents rather than the husband's parents. This preference reflects a practical and cultural tendency for the wife to remain close to her own family after marriage. Given that the wife's parents have a large house with extra rooms, the couple is most likely to live with them. Living with the husband's parents would be less typical in this context. Therefore, the couple will most likely live with the wife's parents.

In Zimbabwe, bringing a fire-related gift like an ashtray, heater, or lighter is not the usual choice for a dinner invitation, unless the host has asked for it. The common expectation is to avoid such items because they are generally seen as inappropriate for this occasion. Instead, the person should choose a gift that is not fire-related, such as food, flowers, or something the host has mentioned needing. This fits the situation because the invitation is for a meal, and a non-fire gift shows thoughtfulness without risking an unwelcome present. Selecting a fire-related item could be seen as a poor choice, so it is better to err on the side of a safe, appreciated gift.

In the United States, emptying the cup completely is not the usual way to signal that you do not want more tea. The common expectation is to leave a small amount of liquid in the cup, which lets the host know you are satisfied and do not need a refill. So the guest should leave a little tea in the cup rather than drinking it all. This small remaining amount is understood as a polite indication that the guest has had enough. Emptying the cup would likely be taken as a sign that the guest would welcome another serving.

In Hong Kong, the idea that each nuclear family commonly lives in its own separate home does not reflect the usual pattern. Maintaining inherited family living arrangements is important there, and it is common for three generations to live together in the same household. For this married couple with a new child, the customary choice would be to contribute to a larger house where the husband's parents also live. Living separately in a small apartment would go against the traditional expectation of keeping the extended family together. Therefore, the couple would live with the husband's parents in a larger house.

In Thailand, crossing the knife and fork on the plate is not the usual way to signal that a meal is finished. The common expectation is to place the knife and fork parallel to each other on the plate. This parallel placement is understood as a clear sign that the person has completed their meal. Therefore, the person should place the knife and fork parallel to each other on the plate. Doing so fits the local dining practice and avoids any confusion about whether more food is desired.

In Bangladesh, the idea that people generally avoid physical contact when greeting someone of the opposite gender is not accurate. Cheek-kissing and hugging are familiar greetings there, and colleagues who are comfortable with such contact would likely use them. So the man and woman would most likely greet each other with a cheek-kiss and a hug. A verbal greeting or a nod would be less fitting for people who are used to these physical greetings.

In Thailand, the idea that a couple may see one another alone or in private during the period of acquaintance before marriage is not the usual expectation. Protecting one's public image and avoiding social disapproval matter a great deal, so a woman is generally expected to avoid being alone with a man she is getting to know. Meeting at his apartment would risk damaging her reputation and could be seen as careless about how others judge her. The woman should decline the invitation to meet at his apartment and continue meeting in public places. This choice preserves her public image and shows that she takes social expectations seriously.

In South Sudan, offering a hand to help an elderly person rise from a seat is not seen as implying incapacity; rather, it is a common and polite gesture of respect. The expectation is to assist the elderly person in getting out of their seat, as this shows care and consideration for their comfort. Therefore, the young adult should offer a hand to help the elderly person stand up. Refraining from doing so would miss an opportunity to show respect and could be perceived as indifferent or impolite. Helping the elderly person is the appropriate action in this situation.

In Hungary, the idea that families commonly encourage all sons to pursue secular careers rather than ordination is not accurate. Maintaining inherited religious practices and beliefs is important, and this often leads families to encourage one son to become a monk. For the youngest son, who has just finished school, the family would most likely encourage him to pursue ordination as a monk. This decision aligns with the tradition of preserving religious heritage within the family. Choosing a secular career would not fit this expectation, as it would overlook the value placed on continuing religious life.

In Afghanistan, a host's invitation to 'stay as long as you like' is not a literal permission to remain indefinitely. It is a polite expression of hospitality, and the guest is expected to read the situation and leave at a reasonable time. When the host glances at the clock, that is a clear signal that the visit has lasted long enough. The guest should therefore take the hint and depart, rather than staying longer. Remaining for as long as one wishes would ignore the host's nonverbal cue and could be seen as inconsiderate.

In Hungary, the expectation that a person should expect direct, straightforward communication to reach an agreement is not accurate. Instead, the common expectation is that communication will be indirect, with parties often responding with general comments and asking about unrelated matters rather than addressing each point directly. In this situation, the first party should expect indirect communication to occur in order to reach an agreement. The other side's general comments and unrelated questions are part of that indirect style, not a sign of disinterest or evasion. Therefore, the first party should not push for direct answers but should work within this indirect communication pattern to move the negotiation forward.

In Israel, the host does not take the seat farthest from the entrance as the most honoured place. The common expectation is that the host sits in the seat closest to the entrance. This position allows the host to welcome guests and manage the flow of the gathering. Therefore, the host should sit in the seat closest to the entrance. Sitting farthest from the entrance would place the host in a position typically reserved for a guest of honor, which is not the host's usual role.

In Cyprus, the idea that a widowed elderly person usually continues living independently in their own home is not the common expectation. When an elderly couple lives independently and one spouse dies, the widowed person is generally expected to move in with their children. In this situation, the woman's adult daughter lives in a nearby town, so the woman should move in with her daughter. Continuing to live alone in her own home would not align with the usual practice in Cyprus, where family members are expected to support one another in times of loss. Moving in with her daughter would provide the care and companionship that is commonly expected in such circumstances.

In Timor-Leste, there is a common expectation to avoid actions that might cause discomfort or inconvenience to others, especially in shared settings like a meal. This means that when dining together, people generally wait until everyone has been served before starting to eat, even if the person who is still waiting insists that others can go ahead. In this situation, the two guests should therefore wait until the third guest's plate is served before beginning to eat. Starting to eat while the third guest is still waiting would risk making that guest feel uncomfortable or left out, which would go against the value of avoiding discomfort to others. Waiting shows consideration for the third guest and maintains a sense of shared participation in the meal.

In Bangladesh, a decision made without giving everyone a chance to speak is not treated as final. The expectation is that if the discussion has not been all-inclusive, structured and detailed, the matter will be brought up again in the next meeting. So the team should not simply move on; they should return to the proposed approach later and make sure the members who have not yet voiced their opinions get a proper opportunity to do so. This keeps the decision-making process open and ensures that all perspectives are considered before a conclusion is reached.

In New Zealand, the idea that neighbors should give a grieving family privacy and only offer help if asked does not reflect the usual practice. Supporting the welfare of close community members during hardship is important, so when a family loses a loved one, the community is expected to come together and help. Neighbors commonly assist with practical tasks such as cooking meals, cleaning the house, or looking after children, rather than waiting to be asked. In this situation, the neighbors should offer to help with meals and other practical tasks. This approach fits the expectation of collective support, whereas waiting for the family to ask would leave them without the help they need at a difficult time.

In Kenya, the idea that extended families are not expected to regularly visit each other or celebrate major occasions together is mistaken. Maintaining close relationships and shared traditions with extended family is important, so relatives are expected to visit one another regularly and to come together for major holidays. For this young couple, that means they should visit their relatives for the holiday. Not visiting would go against the common expectation of staying connected with family and sharing in important celebrations.

In Israel, the idea that the eldest son would simply pursue his own independent life and leave household leadership to the mother or other relatives does not reflect the usual expectation. When a father passes away, the eldest son is commonly expected to step into the role of head of the household. This means he takes on the responsibility of supporting and guiding his mother and younger siblings. In this situation, the eldest son should assume the role of head of the household and support his mother and younger siblings. Pursuing his own independent life would leave the family without the leadership and support that the eldest son is expected to provide.

In Tonga, letting friends pay for a person on multiple occasions is not seen as harmless; it can damage the person's reputation. Protecting one's public image and avoiding humiliation matter a great deal there. When someone repeatedly accepts others' generosity without reciprocating, it signals an inability to meet social expectations and can bring shame. The person should therefore pay for their own share of the upcoming outing. This shows they are not taking advantage of their friends and preserves their standing in the group. Letting friends pay again would risk being seen as dependent or ungrateful, which would reflect poorly on the person.

In Austria, repeating a compliment about a child after it has been acknowledged is not the usual polite practice. The common expectation is to avoid repeating the compliment or continuing to admire the child once the friend has thanked the guest. The guest should therefore not repeat the compliment or continue to admire the child. Doing so could be seen as excessive or as drawing unwanted attention to the child. Instead, the guest should move on to another topic or simply enjoy the visit without further comment on the child.

In Ukraine, declining a second serving with a direct, firm refusal and no bow is not the usual way to handle this. When a guest cannot accept more food, a polite bow is a common way to show respect and gratitude while declining. The guest should bow politely to the host while declining the second serving. This gesture acknowledges the host's generosity and maintains a warm, respectful atmosphere. A direct, firm refusal without a bow could come across as abrupt or ungrateful, which would be less fitting in this setting.

In Palestine, the idea that the most senior person simply takes the first sip without any toast is not how a first drink is usually handled. The common expectation is that before anyone drinks, the group makes a toast together. This shared toast marks the start of the drinking and is a customary part of the occasion. So in this restaurant setting, the colleagues should raise their glasses and offer a toast before taking the first sip. Waiting for the senior person to drink silently would miss that collective gesture. The customary thing to do is to make a toast before anyone takes the first sip.

In Singapore, the idea that personal business relationships should not be used to influence negotiations is not how things usually work. Maintaining and leveraging personal business relationships is important there, and a close friendship with the other side's key decision-maker is exactly the kind of connection that can help move a stalled deal forward. The partner should ask the close friend to intervene and help move the negotiations forward. This fits the situation because the talks have been stuck for weeks and both sides are frustrated, so a personal appeal from a trusted friend can break the deadlock. Proceeding without involving the close friend would miss an opportunity to use a relationship that is meant to be cultivated and relied upon in business.

In South Korea, when a new member's name is announced to a group, the expectation is not that others will introduce themselves by name to that person. Instead, the new member is expected to take the initiative and introduce themselves by name to the other attendees. This means the new member should actively approach others and offer their name, rather than waiting for others to do so. In this situation, the new member should introduce themselves by name to the other attendees. Waiting for others to introduce themselves would not align with the common expectation in South Korea, where the person whose name has been announced is typically the one to initiate introductions.

In Brazil, finishing all the food on one's plate is not the usual way to signal that one does not want a second serving. In some households, the common expectation is the opposite: leaving a small amount of food on the plate shows that the guest is satisfied and does not need more. Therefore, the guest should leave a small amount of food on the plate. This signals to the host that the guest is full and does not want a second serving. Finishing everything might be interpreted as still being hungry and wanting more, which would not match the guest's intention.

In Laos, maintaining inherited family living arrangements is important, and this shapes expectations about when a young adult leaves the parental home. Most children are expected to remain living with their parents until they marry or start their own family, even if they are financially independent. Since the young adult has just finished vocational training and secured a stable job but is not yet married or starting a family, the common expectation would be to continue living with their parents. Moving into their own apartment now, despite being able to afford it, would go against this traditional pattern. Therefore, most people in this situation would be expected to stay with their parents until marriage or starting a family.

In Malaysia, the gesture described is not seen as harmless or playful. Placing the wrist on the inside of the opposite elbow and bending the elbow with a closed fist is commonly understood as a rude or insulting gesture. It is not a casual or friendly motion, so a person making it would likely be perceived as being disrespectful or offensive. Therefore, the gesture would most likely be interpreted as rude or insulting, not as harmless or playful.

In Zimbabwe, arriving empty-handed to a colleague's home for a first dinner party is not the usual expectation. When invited to someone's house for a social occasion or visiting for the first time, it is common to bring a small gift. This gesture shows appreciation for the invitation and respect for the host. Therefore, the person should bring a small gift, such as flowers, sweets, or something modest, to the dinner party. Going without a gift might be seen as lacking thoughtfulness or failing to acknowledge the host's effort.

In Australia, arriving empty-handed to a colleague's home for a first dinner party is not the usual expectation. When invited to someone's house for an occasion or visiting for the first time, it is common to bring a small gift such as flowers, chocolates, or wine. This gesture shows appreciation for the invitation and the host's effort. Therefore, the person should bring a small gift like flowers, chocolates, or wine. Doing so aligns with the local custom of acknowledging hospitality, whereas arriving with nothing might seem inattentive or ungrateful.

In Pakistan, when waiting in a queue, it is commonly expected that a person keeps their belongings from touching the person in front or behind them. This expectation reflects a concern for avoiding actions that might cause discomfort or offense to others. In this situation, the backpack occasionally touching the person in front would likely be seen as rude. The person in front would probably interpret the contact as a lack of consideration for their personal space. Therefore, the person in front would most likely view the backpack touching them as rude rather than acceptable.

In Colombia, when a mutual acquaintance introduces two people, it is generally seen as impolite for one person to ask the acquaintance questions about the other person while that person is standing there. The person being introduced would likely interpret the question as rude, because it suggests the asker is seeking information behind their back rather than engaging with them directly. This expectation reflects a common preference for respectful and considerate introductions, where the focus is on the people meeting rather than on third-party commentary. Therefore, the person being introduced would probably feel that the question was inappropriate in that moment.

In Sudan, the idea that grandparents generally do not move into the same home to help with childcare is not accurate. Supporting the well-being of close family members is important, and this often leads to grandparents moving in with a parent to aid in caring for the children. A customary arrangement would be for the grandparents to move into the same home as the young couple. This allows them to provide direct, daily help with the children while living together. Helping from a separate residence would be less common and would not reflect the usual expectation of close family support in this situation.

In Brazil, the idea that either hand is acceptable for eating and that the left hand is not considered unclean is not accurate. The common expectation is that the left hand is regarded as unclean, so people generally use the right hand for eating. Therefore, the guest should use the right hand to take food from the shared platter. Using the left hand would be seen as inappropriate in this setting.

In Germany, simply saying "excuse me" without any bow is not the usual way to excuse oneself for obstructing someone's view. The common expectation is to accompany the apology with a slight bow. So when the person pauses in front of someone and blocks their view, they should say "excuse me" while giving a slight bow. This small gesture shows acknowledgment of the inconvenience caused. Therefore, the person is expected to say "excuse me" while giving a slight bow.

In Colombia, calling a colleague a 'tzampatzis' after they forgot their wallet is not usually taken as a light-hearted joke. The term carries a strong negative connotation, implying that the person is a free rider or someone who takes advantage of others. In this situation, the colleague who forgot their wallet is being accused of deliberately avoiding payment, which is a serious accusation. Therefore, the remark would most likely be perceived as a serious insult, not as playful teasing. It would probably cause offense and damage the relationship among the colleagues.

In Romania, the idea that a young adult should keep the bond with aunts and uncles weaker than the bond with parents does not reflect the usual expectation. Maintaining close relationships with extended family members is important there, and people are encouraged to make the relationship with aunts and uncles just as strong as the relationship with parents. In this family gathering, the young adult should therefore spend time with the aunt and uncle in a way that builds a relationship equal in strength to the one with their parents. Treating the aunt and uncle as less important would go against the value placed on close extended-family ties. The appropriate approach is to nurture the relationship with the aunt and uncle to be just as strong as the relationship with parents.

In Zimbabwe, a deadlock in negotiations is not usually met with a quick move toward compromise. The expectation is that both sides will hold their positions and wait for the other to show flexibility first. So one partner should expect the other to remain firm and let the impasse stand until the other side signals a willingness to adjust. This is not about stubbornness but about a common preference for letting the other party take the first step toward a solution. Therefore, the partner should not push for a compromise now; instead, they should wait and see if the other side eventually softens.

In Afghanistan, the idea that people are more willing to engage in business deals with those offering the best terms, regardless of personal relationship, does not reflect the usual preference. Reliability and trustworthiness in close relationships are important, so business owners often prefer to work with those they know and trust. A long-time acquaintance with whom the owner has a personal relationship is seen as more dependable than a new company, even if the new company offers a slightly better price. Therefore, the business owner is more likely to choose the long-time acquaintance. Choosing the new company based only on price would overlook the value placed on established trust and could be seen as less reliable in this context.

In Ireland, asking a new colleague about their marital status or salary during a coffee break is not the usual way to get to know someone. Such personal questions are generally considered inappropriate in a workplace setting, especially with someone you have just met. The expectation is to keep the conversation light and professional, avoiding topics that could make the other person uncomfortable. Therefore, the coworker should not ask about marital status or salary. Instead, they might talk about work, hobbies, or general interests. This approach respects the new colleague's privacy and helps build a comfortable working relationship.

In Canada, leaving a small amount of food on the plate is not the usual way to signal satisfaction. The common expectation is that a guest who has finished and does not want more food will leave the plate empty. An empty plate tells the host that the meal was enjoyed and that no additional serving is needed. Therefore, the guest should leave the plate empty. Leaving a small amount of food could be read as a sign that the guest did not like the meal or is still hungry, which would not convey the intended message.

In Pakistan, relying only on the face-to-face meeting and not following up would not keep the business relationship warm. The common expectation is that a person should follow up after a meeting to maintain the warmth of the business relationship. Therefore, the partner should send a follow-up message summarizing the discussion and next steps. This shows continued engagement and helps preserve the positive connection established during the meeting. Not sending a follow-up could be seen as neglecting the relationship, which would be contrary to the value placed on maintaining warm business ties.

In Japan, a business relationship is not meant to stay strictly professional; it is expected to grow into a personal friendship. The sales representative should therefore invite the client to a casual lunch. This fits the situation because the two have already worked together for years and have a friendly rapport, so a personal invitation is a natural next step. Keeping the relationship only professional would miss the chance to deepen the trust that Japanese business culture values.

In Papua New Guinea, a calm and fact-based response to a controversial topic is not what makes the other person less likely to continue the discussion. On the contrary, when the other person remains respectful and intellectually informed, the first colleague is more likely to keep the conversation going. The expectation is that a respectful, well-informed exchange encourages further discussion rather than shutting it down. So in this situation, the first colleague is more likely to continue discussing the topic because the other person responded calmly with facts and studies.

In Tonga, the idea that a buyer should make a single offer close to the bottom-line figure is not how business negotiations usually work there. The common expectation is to make several offers, each moving gradually toward the final price, because prices typically shift by only a small percentage between the initial offer and the final decision. So the buyer should not jump straight to a near-bottom-line offer; that would skip the gradual back-and-forth that is part of the process. Instead, the buyer should make several offers, each moving gradually toward the final price. This approach fits the situation because it respects the local practice of incremental negotiation, allowing both sides to adjust step by step rather than forcing a quick conclusion.

In Portugal, a response like "let me think about that" is not usually a sign that the person is genuinely undecided and needs time to consider. Instead, it is commonly understood as a polite way of declining the request. The colleague should therefore interpret the team member's response as a refusal to take on the additional project. This indirect style of communication is a common expectation in Portuguese professional settings, where people often avoid a direct "no" to preserve harmony and avoid embarrassment. So the colleague should not wait for a later confirmation or assume the team member is still weighing the option; the response itself is the answer.

In Croatia, a new employee is not expected to speak in a direct, frank manner with colleagues they have not worked with before. Most people there feel uncomfortable being direct with those they do not have a strong relationship with. The new employee should therefore express the concern in a gentle, indirect manner, perhaps by framing it as a question or a suggestion rather than a blunt statement. This approach respects the existing social distance and avoids putting colleagues on the spot. A direct, frank manner would likely be seen as too abrupt or even rude in this context.

In Romania, a business partner is not expected to stick rigidly to the terms discussed in a meeting when they have the chance to consult their manager. The common expectation is that a representative may adjust their position between meetings after checking with their superior. Here, the supplier's representative has the opportunity to speak with their manager before the next meeting, so they should do so and then adjust their position based on that consultation. Adhering strictly to the previous terms would miss the chance to align with the manager's guidance and could weaken the supplier's negotiating position. Therefore, the representative should consult the manager and adjust their position accordingly before the next meeting.

In Japan, the expectation that everyone, including upper management, arrives at a meeting on time or slightly early is not how it usually works. It is common for senior managers to arrive late to meetings, and this is generally understood as a normal part of the workplace. Therefore, the senior manager's arrival after 10:15 AM is most likely seen as a normal occurrence for a senior manager, not as a sign of disrespect or a problem. The team would probably not interpret the lateness as a breach of etiquette, but rather as an expected behavior given the manager's position.

In the Philippines, the idea that it is equally acceptable for men and women to be unshaved, slightly unkempt, and out of shape does not reflect the usual expectation. There is a common preference for women to present themselves more neatly, especially at a family gathering. A woman with uncombed hair and a loose, casual outfit is more likely to be seen as less presentable than a man who is unshaved and wearing casual clothes. Therefore, the man's appearance is more acceptable at the gathering. This is because the standard for women's grooming tends to be stricter, and a woman's unkempt look may draw more negative attention.

In Zimbabwe, the claim that the highest-ranking person sits closest to the door is not the usual practice. In large meetings, colleagues from the same company sit on the same side of the table, but the highest-ranking person takes the seat furthest from the door. This arrangement places the most senior person in the position of greatest authority and visibility. Therefore, the colleagues should sit on the same side of the table, with the highest-ranking person furthest from the door. Sitting closest to the door would be seen as less appropriate for the senior member.

In Malta, a seating arrangement or speaking order is not something to be ignored; it carries real weight in a business setting. Following formal procedures and rules matters there, so the chairs and name cards are meant to be respected. The junior employee should therefore take the seat indicated by the name card. Sitting wherever they prefer would disregard the established order and could be seen as failing to observe proper protocol. Taking the assigned seat shows awareness of the meeting's structure and respect for the organizers' intentions.

In Australia, independent adults generally value their privacy and prefer not to share their real-time location with family members.
